doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Arriving in New York with a bass, a suitcase and Murray Wall's number
summary: She came on a grant, intending a summer stay, aged 24, with only one phone number; she worked in fashion and played a lunchtime gig with Gloria Coleman.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. Okay. Well you were able to come to the United States on a grant?
At that time did you think you know what — I think I could make a living at this. Did you come here with that idea or did it sort of evolve?

Well that’s a good question because who knows. When you come to a city like New York, I mean you really have to know that once you emigrate to a country where things are done slightly different than Australia, it’s really, I like that expression “get in line.” Look how many bass players have really made their mark in New York City, and have for a long time, have great reputations. So it was really like get to the back of the line, unless you came to New York already knowing twenty people that were going to immediately — but I actually just came with a bass and a suitcase and I had a phone number in my book for Murray Wall.

And so no, I didn’t know if I was going to — I really left Australia saying I’m just going for the summer, the New York summer, the American summer, I’m just going for a few months, I’ll see you maybe in October or November. Very vague. It totally scared the life out of my parents. You know I was 24, and just brave I guess. Crazy or brave, I don’t know which one. But I rose to the challenge. Soon after I met this Australian girl and I worked in fashion for eight months. Because I really didn’t know if I was ever going to get — you know I had a gig with George Coleman Junior’s mother, Gloria Coleman, who © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

is a wonderful piano player. I think it paid like 30 bucks or something like that. It was like a lunchtime gig at the Film Center. So I did Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday I worked in fashion selling prints to fashion designers. And that world was crazy. That was a crazy world. The whole fashion world. Skinny girls and gay guys pretty much. So I thought well, this is something different. You know, very competitive and but interesting kind of, it was creative. And so I did that for eight months. And I sold all these prints [inaudible] paisleys, whatever the fashion designers, you know, prints on paper. Sales. It was hard work. It was my first job. So I did that for a while and then on Thursday and Friday I did lunchtimes with George Coleman Junior on drums and Gloria Coleman on piano, at the Film Center in New York.
